description: Discriminator: request completion against an inactive node. Three nodes are created by NewRaft from the captured source and shut down through the public Shutdown(); Shutdown().Error() returns only after the raft goroutine group (run, runFSM, runSnapshots) has exited, so no handler remains. Then the public client APIs are called on the inactive instances: 128 VerifyLeader calls on a default-configured node, whose verifyCh is buffered with 64 slots, and 128 Apply calls on a node configured with the documented BatchApplyCh option, whose applyCh is buffered. Observation: for every call the harness records whether the API returned ErrRaftShutdown immediately or returned a future, and after a bounded wait it non-blockingly inspects each returned future's own completion channel; the asserted field is the total number of returned futures that had still not completed, and per-path counts are reported beside it. Control: the same select structure is exercised on a default-configured node whose applyCh is unbuffered (Barrier), where the send case can never be ready; that node completes every call, which separates the buffering of the channel from the API and from the shutdown state.

harness.description: TestAssuranceInactiveRequestCompletion: VerifyLeader and batched Apply issued after Shutdown completed, with an unbuffered Barrier control
semantic_changes: No target file is modified; the harness adds one external test file to the captured package. Nodes are created by the package's own NewRaft over the in-memory store and transport and are shut down through the public Shutdown().

The harness inspects each returned future's own completion channel non-blockingly instead of calling Error(), because Error() would block on exactly the futures under investigation. That read is sound here only because the writer is a raft handler and Shutdown().Error() has already joined every raft goroutine.
The bounded 250 ms wait corroborates the observation but is not the property; permanence rests on the shutdown join, which the plan states as the legality argument rather than as a measured timeout.
The third node is a diagnostic control that shares the select structure but has an unbuffered channel; it is not part of the asserted comparison.

legality.derivation: VerifyLeader, ApplyLog and Barrier each select between r.shutdownCh and a send on an internal request channel (s-api-verify-leader, s-api-apply-select, s-api-barrier-select). verifyCh is created with 64 slots (s-api-verify-ch-buffer) and applyCh is buffered whenever BatchApplyCh is set (s-api-apply-buffer). Shutdown closes shutdownCh, run returns on it, and shutdownFuture.Error then calls waitShutdown, which waits for the goroutine group containing run, runFSM and runSnapshots (s-raft-run-shutdown, s-state-wait-shutdown, s-future-shutdown-future); the only producer of responses for these channels is the main loop's verify and apply cases (s-raft-verify-mainloop). The futures cannot escape by another route because deferError.Error waits on errCh or ShutdownCh and neither logFuture nor verifyFuture sets ShutdownCh (s-future-defer-error). The documented result for operations against an inactive Raft is ErrRaftShutdown (s-api-err-shutdown) and the in-repo after-shutdown test asserts that everything should fail while its TODO records that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck (s-test-after-shutdown). The harness creates the nodes with the package's own NewRaft, shuts them down with the public Shutdown(), and only then issues the calls, so the prefix contains a completed join and an inactive node state rather than a timing assumption.
legality.applicability: Applies to the default configuration through VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered, and to ApplyLog under the documented BatchApplyCh option; the diagnostic control uses the default unbuffered applyCh. No fault injection, clock manipulation or target-file modification is used, and the harness exercises the public client API of the captured implementation.
unresolved: the select between an already-closed shutdown channel and a buffered send is a schedule choice, so the number of unresolved futures varies between runs and a schedule in which every call took the shutdown branch would report holds
the exact repair location remains open: drain the buffered channels during shutdown, set deferError.ShutdownCh for these futures, or stop offering the send case once shutdown is signalled
a request enqueued before shutdown rather than issued after it is outside this prefix
conflicts: the after-shutdown test asserts that everything should fail while its own TODO comment records that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck instead
alternatives: the send-before-shutdown ordering could be attributed to the caller racing shutdown, but ErrRaftShutdown is documented for operations against an inactive Raft and VerifyLeader and Barrier expose no timeout, so the completion duty stays with the library

grounding.derivation: The result event is emitted only after both shutdown calls returned and after every request had been issued and inspected, so the observation covers the whole prefix. The prerequisite records that the nodes reached the Shutdown state through Shutdown().Error(), which joins the raft goroutine group (s-state-wait-shutdown), and the futures inspected are the ones the public APIs returned (s-api-verify-leader, s-api-apply-select); their only completion channel is errCh, which deferError consults together with ShutdownCh (s-future-defer-error). A call that returned ErrRaftShutdown is a completed call and is counted as such (s-api-err-shutdown), so the count of unresolved futures is exactly the number of client requests whose completion is still owed.
grounding.applicability: Same nodes, same shutdown state and same prefix as the harness; the diagnostic control node is reported alongside but does not share the asserted premise.
unresolved: whether the observed unresolved futures would remain unresolved indefinitely is argued from the shutdown join rather than measured; the bounded wait only shows they did not complete during it

observable_properties.description: Every client request issued against the inactive nodes must have completed, so the number of returned futures that still had not completed after the requests were issued must be zero. The field is a direct count of owed completions - calls that returned ErrRaftShutdown are counted as completed, and per-path counts (unresolved_verify, unresolved_apply) plus the unbuffered Barrier control are reported beside it as diagnostics. The predicate is the requirement's own completion demand rather than a proxy: it does not compare values of different kinds and it does not filter the result through applicability.

uncertainties: Permanence rests on the shutdown join, not on the wait: Shutdown().Error() calls waitShutdown, which waits for the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines, so after it returns no writer exists for the futures' channels. The 250 ms wait only corroborates that none of them completed.

The select between an already-closed shutdown channel and a send on a buffered channel is a schedule choice, so the unresolved counts vary between runs (64/64, 64/59 and 57/54 in construction runs); a schedule in which every call took the shutdown branch would report holds, and the fixed prefix does not eliminate that schedule, only makes it vanishingly unlikely.

ApplyLog and Barrier are configuration-dependent: with the default unbuffered applyCh the send case can never be ready, so only the BatchApplyCh option exercises the buffered instance. The Barrier control on the default configuration completes every time.

Only the VerifyLeader and ApplyLog entry points are exercised. The snapshot, bootstrap, configuration-change and restore channels are unbuffered in the captured source and are not part of this prefix, and a request enqueued before shutdown rather than issued after it remains outside it.

The harness reads the futures as live objects through their own completion channel; that read is sound only because the shutdown join has removed every producer, and the harness deliberately does not call Error() so it cannot consume or fabricate a response.
